title: The Muscle Behind Puppy-Dog Eyes
central_question: Why do dogs have that expressive inner-eyebrow look?
central_fact: Dogs have a facial muscle that raises the inner eyebrow, and the dogs studied produced that movement more often and intensely than wolves.
takeaway: Puppy-dog eyes are built into dog anatomy. The idea that humans selected for them is a strong hypothesis, not a proven cause.

hook.text: Puppy-dog eyes are anatomy, not just charm.

scenes.narration: Puppy-dog eyes are anatomy, not just charm.

visual.description: A medium-sized brown mixed-breed dog looks up toward an off-screen person, inner eyebrows slightly raised, eyes soft and relaxed. The expression is natural, not exaggerated or tearful. Warm window light and a simple home background.
visual.subject: one brown mixed-breed dog with a white chest patch and expressive brows
visual.motion: slow push-in; the dog's inner brows lift slightly
visual.framing: vertical 9:16, eyes on the upper-third line, caption-safe lower third
visual.continuity: same dog, coat, and warm home setting throughout

scenes.narration: That inner-brow lift comes from a small muscle: the levator anguli oculi medialis, above the inner corner of the eye.

visual.description: An extreme macro of the same dog's eye and inner brow. The fur moves subtly as the brow lifts. A soft translucent highlight traces the area above the inner corner of the eye without any labels or arrows.
visual.subject: the same brown dog's right eye and inner eyebrow
visual.motion: very slow lateral drift, shallow focus
visual.framing: vertical 9:16, eye in the center, brow near the top third
visual.continuity: same eye color, white chest fur at frame edge, same lighting direction

scenes.narration: In 2019, researchers dissected four wolves and six dogs. The muscle was consistently present in the dogs they examined, and not in the wolves.

visual.description: A calm split composition: the same brown dog in a home doorway on one side, a gray wolf standing in a snowy forest on the other. Both are shown alive and unhurried, in profile, with natural fur and correct anatomy. No dissection imagery.
visual.shot_type: two static profile portraits, split screen
visual.subject: the same brown dog and a gray wolf, separate animals
visual.motion: almost still; slight breathing and ear movement
visual.framing: vertical 9:16 split horizontally, dog above wolf, each face in its own half
visual.continuity: dog matches previous scenes; wolf has natural gray coat and yellow eyes

scenes.narration: Dogs also produced the eyebrow movement more often and more intensely than wolves. The highest intensities appeared only in dogs.

visual.description: The same brown dog stands at a shelter-style kennel gate, calmly watching a visitor. The dog's inner brows lift and relax in a natural rhythm. The visitor is visible only as a soft shoulder and hand, never looming or teasing.
visual.shot_type: medium shot through an open kennel gate
visual.subject: the same brown dog and a visitor's shoulder and hand
visual.motion: gentle handheld observation, no sudden moves
visual.framing: vertical 9:16, dog centered behind the gate, visitor's shoulder at the edge
visual.continuity: same dog and coat; kennel is clean, dry, and calm

scenes.narration: The team suggests this may have given dogs an edge: a face that pulls at human sympathy. It is a hypothesis, not a proven cause.

visual.description: A warm living-room scene: the same dog sits beside a seated owner, looking up with a mild inner-brow lift. The owner's hand rests nearby, open and relaxed. The camera stays neutral and does not manufacture sadness.
visual.shot_type: medium two-shot, owner seen from the shoulders down
visual.subject: the same brown dog and an owner's relaxed hand and torso
visual.motion: slow dolly-in toward the dog's face
visual.framing: vertical 9:16, dog's face in the middle third, owner's hand in the lower third
visual.continuity: same dog, living room, and oatmeal sweater as the opening

scenes.narration: What is clear is that the muscle is part of dog anatomy, not a human invention. And the look works on us. Evolution shaped the plea; we answered it.

visual.description: A final portrait of the same brown dog resting on a rug, chin down, eyes open and calm. The camera pulls back slowly to include the owner's hand resting nearby. A brief, tasteful cross-dissolve shows a wolf on a distant ridge, then returns to the dog.
visual.shot_type: low medium shot, then slow pull-back
visual.subject: the same brown dog, an owner's hand, and a distant wolf silhouette
visual.framing: vertical 9:16, dog in the lower middle third, open space above
visual.continuity: same rug and dog; wolf remains a distant separate animal, not a hybrid

claims.text: The levator anguli oculi medialis muscle was consistently present in the dogs dissected and was not present as a separate muscle in the wolves.
claims.limits: Four wolves and six dogs were dissected; one husky specimen lacked a locatable LAOM, and the sample is small.

claims.text: Dogs produced the inner-eyebrow movement more often and at higher intensity than wolves.
claims.limits: The 27 dogs were mainly shelter Staffies and the 9 wolves lived in parks, so setting and sample composition may affect the comparison.

claims.text: The highest-intensity inner-eyebrow movements were produced exclusively by dogs in the study.
claims.limits: This is a sample result, not a claim that no individual wolf can ever produce a strong movement.

claims.text: The authors hypothesize that humans preferred dogs with expressive eyebrows, giving those dogs a selection advantage.
claims.limits: The study documents anatomy and behavior; it does not directly observe human selection or measure fitness over generations.

claims.text: The muscle difference is anatomical, while the story of human-driven selection remains a hypothesis.
claims.limits: Anatomy is directly observed; the evolutionary cause is inferred from the pattern and does not exclude other pressures.

visual_policy.style: Naturalistic, warm documentary illustration with macro facial detail and restrained split-screen comparisons.
visual_policy.anatomy: One brown mixed-breed dog with a white chest patch and consistent brows. The wolf is a separate gray wolf with correct facial proportions, yellow eyes, and a natural coat. No hybrids.
visual_policy.welfare: All animals are calm and alive. No dissection, injury, restraint, kennel distress, or staged sadness. The shelter scene is clean, dry, and non-threatening.
visual_policy.continuity: Same dog, sweater, rug, and lighting across home scenes; the wolf appears only in separate natural settings.
visual_policy.disclosure: Illustrative, AI-assisted visuals; not documentary footage.

notes: Do not say the muscle is absent in every wolf without the sample qualifier; the study examined four wolves.
Label the selection story as a hypothesis on screen and in narration.
Avoid dissection footage; the visual comparison should use living animals and abstract highlights.

risk_notes: The behavioral samples differ by setting and breed, so the comparison is not a controlled laboratory experiment.
Do not imply dogs consciously manipulate people; the anatomy is inherited and the expression can still be used socially.
